raw.answer: A Taipei court judge asked the Constitutional Court whether two immigration-law provisions are constitutional. One bans charging or agreeing on a fee for matchmaking cross-border marriages, and the other fines people who do so. The court decided both provisions do not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: The ban on requiring or agreeing on payment for cross-border marriage matchmaking does not violate the constitutional protections of the right to work, freedom of contract, or equality. The fine of NT$200,000 to NT$1,000,000 for doing so does not violate the constitutional protection of property rights.

points.text: The ban limits the right to work of professional matchmakers and the freedom of contract of occasional matchmakers, but the state may limit these for legitimate public interests if the means reasonably relate to the goal.

The purpose is legitimate: to protect the people marrying, prevent human trafficking, and avoid commodifying marriage and objectifying women, given differences between the parties and information gaps.

The means are reasonably related: the ban does not prohibit matchmaking itself or set qualifications, still allows non-profit matchmaking, and does not bar gifts freely given after success, while helping de-commercialize matchmaking and reduce abuses.
On equality, the court used a lenient standard because the classification is not suspect and involves only commercial matters, not vital personal rights.

Treating cross-border matchmaking worse than domestic matchmaking has a legitimate aim and a reasonable link, since the risks of information gaps, trafficking and pressure on the spouse who relocates are more pronounced.
The fine range lets the authority weigh how serious the violation is, and general rules on reducing penalties can avoid overly harsh results even at the minimum, so property rights are not violated.

raw.answer: A man whose law was struck down as unconstitutional by the court (Interpretation No. 716) kept being turned away when he tried to reopen his old case, partly because the 5-year limit for reopening had passed while his request was pending at the court. The court decided that the time his request was pending at the court should not count toward that 5-year limit. It also let him file again to reopen his case within 30 days.
raw.held: For people whose requests led the court to strike down a law, the time their request was pending at the court does not count toward the maximum period for reopening their case; the same applies to the civil procedure 5-year limit, and Interpretation No. 209 is supplemented to that extent. The applicant may file to reopen the Taipei High Administrative Court judgment within 30 days of this ruling, free of the 5-year limit.

points.text: Interpretations bind everyone and apply to the person who requested them, who may rely on them to seek a reopened case, in order to protect the right to bring lawsuits.
The 5-year maximum for reopening serves the public interest and legal stability and is a reasonable limit in ordinary cases.

But if the time a request is pending at the court counted, a person who wins a favorable interpretation could still be too late and get no effective remedy, so that time must be deducted; any remaining time, or the 30 days from publication if the remainder is longer, applies.

Interpretation No. 209's 5-year limit under the civil procedure rule is similar, so on the same reasoning the pending time is deducted there too and No. 209 is supplemented; its 30-day part needs no change.
The court may set a specific remedy for the underlying case, not bound by the 5-year limit, to give the applicant a real chance of relief.

Even after deducting the pending periods, this applicant would still be past 5 years, after three earlier attempts were rejected, so the court allowed a new filing within 30 days and ordered the case retried in line with Interpretation No. 716.

who: Applicants whose requests led the court to strike down a law
The applicant in this case (莊水池)

raw.answer: Several Indigenous people were prosecuted for hunting-related offences, including possessing guns and hunting wildlife without permission, and they and two courts asked Taiwan's Constitutional Court to review the laws. The court held that Indigenous hunting is a constitutionally protected cultural right that must be balanced against protecting wildlife and the environment. It upheld some rules, found others unconstitutional, and told the authorities to fix the self-made hunting gun definition within 2 years.
raw.held: The rule that decriminalizes only self-made hunting guns is constitutional and clear enough, and requiring advance approval for hunting is constitutional. The self-made hunting gun definition is inadequate and must be revised within 2 years. The fixed 5-day deadline for unforeseeable non-regular hunts and the requirement to list animal species and numbers in applications are unconstitutional and no longer apply. "Traditional culture" in the wildlife law includes non-profit personal use.

points.text: Indigenous people have a constitutional right to live by their traditional culture, and hunting is an important part of it. But this right can be limited by law to protect wildlife, since environmental protection is also a key constitutional value.

Limiting the criminal exemption to self-made hunting guns, and not covering other guns such as air guns, is a legislative policy choice. It reflects reasonable considerations about public order, so it does not violate proportionality. The words "self-made hunting gun" are understandable and courts can interpret them, so the rule is clear enough.

The ministry's definition of self-made hunting guns is crude and has no safety verification or training. This risks deaths and injuries to hunters and third parties, so it falls short of the state's duty to let Indigenous people hunt safely.
"Traditional culture" must include food and life practices passed down in a tribe, such as non-profit personal use. Protected species should generally be excluded, except in special cases.

Requiring advance approval for hunting serves the important goals of protecting ecosystems and third-party safety. No equally effective, less intrusive alternative exists, so the rule is proportionate.
The fixed 5-day deadline for non-regular hunts has no flexibility for sudden, unforeseeable needs. This pushes people to give up their right or break the law, so it goes too far.

Requiring applicants to state in advance the species and number of animals conflicts with traditional taboos. It adds little to the goals, since authorities can set limits themselves, so it is unconstitutional.

raw.answer: Judges and people sentenced in several cases asked whether 'compulsory labor' (a security measure that confines people in a labor facility, in addition to prison) is constitutional under the Criminal Code, the Theft and Receiving Stolen Goods Act, and the Organized Crime Prevention Act. The Constitutional Court held that all of these rules wrongly limit personal liberty. The rules still in force lost effect from the date of the ruling.
raw.held: The current Criminal Code, theft-act and organized-crime-act compulsory labor rules violate the proportionality principle and the guarantee of personal liberty (the organized-crime rule also fails the clear-separation principle), and they lose effect from the ruling's announcement. Compulsory labor not yet carried out or not yet finished is waived, and time spent waiting in the labor facility to serve a prison term counts toward that term.

points.text: Compulsory labor confines people and is much like a prison sentence, so it must pass strict proportionality review, and as a security measure it must be clearly separated from punishment.

The Criminal Code rules pursue an important aim, but the labor content and skills training can be done during the prison term, and the offender-protection system helps more without confinement, so compulsory labor is not the least harmful means. A fixed 3 years regardless of the case's seriousness is also excessive.
The theft-act rules use the same means and likewise are not the least harmful. Those targeted often already get longer prison terms, and the fixed 3-year term ignores the circumstances of each case.

The organized-crime rules apply to everyone convicted regardless of personality or circumstances, and a fixed 3 years (or 5 years under the 1996 version) is not the least harmful means. Waiver mechanisms are rarely used in practice.

The organized-crime rules also use compulsory labor to add deterrence to punishment, with no purpose or conditions distinct from punishment. This amounts to a double deprivation of liberty and fails the clear-separation principle.

In practice, compulsory labor is not clearly separated from prison. Supervision and visits are similar, it is carried out in the same place as prison terms, and the people held do the same work and training as prisoners, with no special corrective assessment.

who: Prisoners who must still serve a prison term
Courts and judges applying these rules
Petitioners whose final judgments applied these rules

raw.answer: A teacher in the public servants' insurance (公保) scheme was dismissed, and the dismissal was later cancelled by a court. She was reinstated and asked to be insured retroactively for the gap period, but the authority refused for the stretches when she was also in labor insurance. The court held that the ban on double insurance is constitutional, but in this special situation the double-insured years must count toward the old-age benefit.
raw.held: The rules banning double enrollment in public servants' insurance and other social insurance are not unconstitutional. But for people reinstated after an unlawful dismissal was cancelled, the years of double coverage must be counted as insured years for the old-age benefit, and the authority must handle the petitioner's retroactive enrollment request accordingly.

points.text: Old-age benefits under public servants' insurance are protected property rights, but the legislature has wide freedom to design social insurance and may limit them if the means reasonably relate to the purpose.

The ban on double insurance aims to avoid wasting public resources through double subsidies and to avoid the incentive to claim twice for one insured event. This is a legitimate aim reasonably served by the rules, so they meet the proportionality principle and do not violate property rights.

When an unlawful dismissal is cancelled it is void retroactively, so the reason for the forced withdrawal never existed, and the person may be restored as insured and enrolled retroactively with the years counted.
Double coverage in this situation was caused by official action and not by the insured person's fault, so it differs from ordinary double enrollment.

Refusing to count those years would reduce the person's right to the old-age benefit, and the legislature has made no rule for this case. The years must therefore be counted, and the 'years not recognized' clause does not cover this situation.
The challenge to two Ministry letters was not accepted, because they were replies on individual matters and are not 'orders' that can be reviewed.

who: Public servants and teachers reinstated after an unlawful dismissal was cancelled
Insured people who joined other social insurance during the forced withdrawal

raw.answer: A parent whose minor daughter was harmed by three juveniles asked the court to review a rule on juvenile hearings that gave victims no chance to speak in court. The Constitutional Court found that the juvenile case law, taken as a whole, does not expressly let victims (or their legal representatives) appear and give their views, and this falls short of constitutional due process. The government must fix the law within 2 years, and until then juvenile courts must generally summon victims to speak.
raw.held: Article 36 and the related provisions of the Juvenile Case Act, read together, are unconstitutional to the extent they do not expressly let victims (and their legal representatives) appear in court and state their views in juvenile protection cases. The responsible authorities must amend the law within 2 years, and until then juvenile courts must summon victims and give them a chance to speak, unless there is a proper reason it is unsuitable.

points.text: The constitutional right to sue and the due process principle give crime victims, including victims in juvenile cases, a basic right to take part in court proceedings, including appearing to state their views.

The state must specially protect the healthy growth of children and youth, and the Juvenile Case Act aims at the juvenile's healthy self-development, so juvenile protection proceedings differ from criminal trials, but victims keep a right to speak where this does not conflict with that aim.

Victim statements help the court find the facts and choose suitable protective measures, and the Act has long given victims their own procedural standing, such as receiving rulings, appealing and consenting to apology or restoration steps.

So lawmakers must balance protecting juveniles with victims' participation, at minimum giving victims a chance to state views in court, and may not exclude them across the board without proper reason and proportionality.

Article 36 only gives the juvenile's legal representative, guardian and assistant a chance to speak, and other provisions only occasionally let victims speak when consent is sought, so victims have no regular right to be heard.

As a result victims may be unable to give their account or views to the court, so the rules fail due process; the court ordered a 2-year fix and interim summoning of victims, with the court choosing a manner of speaking that respects the juvenile's healthy growth.

who: Victims of juvenile misconduct and their legal representatives
Legislators and authorities amending the law

raw.answer: A Taipei court was hearing a case where a company that won a government contract owed about NT$2.95 million in a fee for not hiring enough indigenous employees, although the contract was worth only NT$1.64 million. The Constitutional Court found that the law's one-size-fits-all formula for this fee is unconstitutional where it produces clearly excessive amounts, because it has no adjustment mechanism.
raw.held: The fixed formula (shortfall in headcount times monthly minimum wage) violates the constitution to the extent it has no adjustment for clearly excessive cases, such as a fee above the contract value. The authorities must amend it within 2 years, and until then they and the courts must handle such cases appropriately.

points.text: A fee imposed for failing to meet a legal duty still limits property rights, so it must meet the constitution's proportionality requirement.
Where the fee exceeds the contract value, a reduction mechanism is appropriate to avoid seriously harming property rights in unusual cases.
The earlier ruling already found the hiring-quota and fee-payment rules themselves not unconstitutional.
The formula's purpose of encouraging winning bidders to hire indigenous people is legitimate, and the method helps achieve it.

The formula ignores whether the company is not at fault and how large the contract is, so the fee can exceed the contract value and go beyond a reasonable burden; the legislature had not fixed this despite an earlier call.
Because the uniform formula has no adjustment for clearly excessive cases, it is disproportionate to that extent and unconstitutional.

who: Courts and agencies applying the law

raw.answer: A licensed Taipei street performer had his permit revoked after repeated violations, and he challenged the city rules that require street performers to get a permit after being reviewed. The court found that the permit system was set up without the required legal basis, and that reviewing a performer's skill or the content of their act violates constitutional freedoms. Reviewing whether an act suits a designated public space was found acceptable.
raw.held: The three permit rules, taken together, violate the rule that restrictions on rights need a legal basis, because they were not passed by the local legislature or authorized by a local ordinance. The parts that review performers' skill or the content of their acts are unconstitutional, while the part that checks whether an act suits a designated public space is not.

points.text: The permit rules limit occupational freedom and artistic expression, so they needed a local ordinance passed by the local legislature or clear authorization from one. They were only administrative rules issued by the city government, so they violate the principle that restrictions need a legal basis.
Street performing can be a livelihood, and artistic expression is protected as free expression of high value, so both freedoms are protected.

Reviewing performers' skill limits who may choose this occupation. The aim of keeping poor performers off the street offers quality entertainment but is not an important public interest like protecting life or health, so this part violates the freedom to choose an occupation.

Rules on the time, place and manner of performing, including whether an act suits a designated space, only regulate how the job is carried out. They serve the legitimate aim of keeping public spaces orderly and safe, so they do not violate the proportionality principle.

Reviewing performance quality or content is a direct intervention that needs strict scrutiny. Artistic value is a personal judgment the government should not replace, and weak skill does little harm to the public, so the aim is not a especially important public interest and this part violates freedom of artistic expression.

The review of suitability for the space has no hidden aim of suppressing expression, affects content only incidentally, and leaves applicants enough chance to show their skills, so it is not disproportionate.

who: Taipei city government and its permit authority
Public users of Taipei public spaces

raw.answer: A man sentenced to life imprisonment had been held in detention for 985 days before his sentence became final, but a criminal law rule only counted the days beyond the first year (365 days) toward the time served before parole could be requested. The Constitutional Court held that the rule violates the constitutional equality principle, because it treats life-sentence prisoners worse than fixed-term prisoners without a sufficiently justified link to its purpose.
raw.held: The part of the rule that does not count pre-final-judgment detention of under one year toward the time already served for life-sentence parole violates the equality principle (Article 7) and loses effect from the day of the ruling. All pre-judgment detention days must therefore be counted in full.

points.text: Equality requires like cases to be treated alike. Because detention seriously limits personal liberty, a difference in how detention days are counted needs a mid-level review: an important public purpose and a substantial link between the means and that purpose.

The rule creates a difference in treatment: for life-sentence prisoners only detention beyond one year counts toward time served for parole, while for fixed-term prisoners detention days are credited.
The purpose of the difference, keeping life and fixed-term sentences distinct in nature and fair, was accepted as an important public interest.

Parole serves the same goal for both types of sentence, and the law already separates them through very different minimum terms to serve (at least 25 years for life, versus generally half the fixed term), so there is little risk of confusing them.
Detention restricts a person's liberty in the same way whichever sentence follows, so once detention days are counted at all, life-sentence prisoners should not be clearly disadvantaged.

The fear that counting all detention days would make life and fixed terms indistinguishable, or allow parole without entering prison, does not hold, given detention limits and the long time needed to reach the required progressive-treatment grade. So the means lack a substantial link to the purpose.

who: Life-sentence prisoners who were detained before final judgment

raw.answer: The case asked whether a labor law rule barring employers from having women work between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. (unless a union or labor-management meeting agreed and safety and transport conditions were met) violates the constitution's guarantee of gender equality. The court decided that it does, because the rule treats women worse than men without a close enough link to its goals. The rule loses effect from the day the ruling was announced.
raw.held: Article 49, paragraph 1 of the Labor Standards Act, which restricts women's night work, violates the constitutional guarantee of gender equality and ceases to have effect from the date of the ruling's announcement.

points.text: Because the rule treats people differently by sex, the court applied intermediate-level strict review: the goal must serve an important public interest and the means must be substantially related to that goal.
The rule bars women from night work by default and lets them work only with union or labor-management meeting consent, while men face no such limit, so it disadvantages women.
The goals (women's safety, health, stable population structure and generational health) are important public interests.
On safety, the state has a duty to protect women at night through measures such as required transport or housing, not by banning their night work, so the means lack a real link to the goal.

On health, avoiding night work matters for all workers, women are not necessarily harmed more than men, and the household-burden argument reinforces stereotypes and is irrelevant for single or childless women.

Requiring union or labor-management meeting consent is also not substantially related to the goal, since women's suitability for night work varies individually and such bodies may not legitimately speak for each woman.

raw.answer: Several judges and one defendant asked Taiwan's Constitutional Court whether parts of the Copyright Act's criminal rules on illegal copying and selling or distributing pirated discs were unconstitutional. They challenged the word "copying" as vague, the minimum 6-month prison term, the higher fines and penalties for discs, and the rule that these offenses are prosecuted without the victim's complaint. The court found none of these provisions unconstitutional, while suggesting the authorities review the disc-specific heavier penalties.
raw.held: The court held that the word "copying" in Articles 91(2), 91(3) and 91-1(3) is clear enough, and that the 6-month minimum prison term does not violate Article 8 on personal liberty. It also held that the higher disc-related fines and minimum penalties, and the rule in Article 100 making the disc offenses prosecutable without a complaint, do not violate the equality guarantee in Article 7.

points.text: The word "copying" means making a repeat copy. It is understandable, clearly different from adapting a work, and people can foresee what it covers, so it is not unconstitutionally vague.
The 6-month minimum prison term serves an important public interest: protecting authors and the industries around them from more harmful for-sale or disc piracy.

Heavier minimum sentences for these more harmful acts are mostly for the legislature to decide. Courts can still set different sentences case by case and reduce the sentence for minor cases, so the minimum is not disproportionate.

Higher fines and minimum prison terms for discs treat disc offenses differently, but at the time of the amendments discs were the main form of piracy and highly harmful. The distinction served an important purpose and was substantially related to it.
The court noted that discs are no longer the main medium for illegal copying, so the authorities should review whether to keep the heavier disc penalties.

Making the disc offenses prosecutable without a victim's complaint serves a legitimate public interest, because the harm spreads to many rights holders and to the economic order. Treating discs differently reasonably helps prosecute these more serious offenses.

who: People accused of illegally copying or selling pirated discs
Legislature and authorities reviewing the law

raw.answer: A Taoyuan district court judge, hearing two public-order cases, asked whether a person can be fined under the Social Order Maintenance Act after already being prosecuted for the same act under criminal law. The Constitutional Court said no where the person has already been convicted by a final judgment, because that is double punishment. That part of the fine rule loses effect from the date of the ruling.
raw.held: Where the same act has already been prosecuted under criminal law and ended in a final guilty judgment, the proviso in Article 38 allowing an additional fine is double punishment, violates the principle of no double punishment for one offense, and ceases to have effect from the ruling's announcement.

points.text: The principle bars the state from pursuing and punishing the same criminal act twice. It rests on legal stability, protection of reliance and proportionality, and it can also apply to administrative penalties that are equal or similar to criminal punishment in nature, purpose and effect.

The Act's offenses already include minor-crime conduct comparable to criminal offenses. Its penalty factors match those of the Criminal Code, and courts hearing its cases apply the Code of Criminal Procedure where the Act is silent.
So the wrongs and harms under the Act and the criminal offense for the same act differ only in degree, not in essential nature.
Allowing a fine after a final guilty judgment for the same act is therefore double punishment and conflicts with the principle.
The ruling does not decide whether a fine is allowed after a final acquittal, and it finds no conflict in business suspension, closure orders and confiscation, which aim to remove or prevent harm.

who: People already convicted by a final judgment for an act that also breaches the Social Order Maintenance Act
Courts handling Social Order Maintenance Act fine cases

raw.answer: A temple owner (the petitioner) owned land under a building owned by someone else, and the building was registered as a historic building without the landowner's consent. The court held that registration without the landowner's consent is not by itself unconstitutional. But where the landowner's use of the land is restricted beyond what they should bear, the landowner must be fairly compensated, and the current tax breaks are not enough.
raw.held: Registering a historic building without the consent of the owner of the land under it is not easily found to violate the constitutional property right. But where the restrictions amount to a special sacrifice, the tax-break provisions fail to give fair compensation to that landowner and are unconstitutional to that extent. The responsible authorities must amend the law within 2 years of the ruling.

points.text: The constitutional property right covers more than outright seizure. If the state limits use, income or disposal of land beyond the owner's social responsibility, creating a special sacrifice, the owner must be compensated.

Protecting historic buildings serves a legitimate public purpose. A building cannot be separated from its land, so the landowner shares the restrictions, and these are necessary whether or not the owner consents.
So not requiring the landowner's consent for registration is not easily seen as violating the property right.

Once a building on a third party's land is registered, limits on the landowner's use, management and disposal of the land may exceed what they must tolerate. That is a special sacrifice and the owner is entitled to fair compensation, in money or another suitable form, with the legislature free to choose how.
The land-value tax reduction of up to 50% and the inheritance tax exemption are not fair compensation, since they reflect ability-to-pay taxation or are at most tax preferences.
Because those provisions give no fair compensation to such landowners, they do not meet the property-right guarantee to that extent, and the law must be amended within 2 years.

who: Owners of land under registered historic buildings owned by others
Authorities that register historic buildings and amend the law

raw.answer: A real estate appraiser was disciplined for setting up a branch office, which the Real Estate Appraisers Act bars, and he asked the court whether the ban is unconstitutional. The court decided the ban is constitutional and does not violate the constitutional protection of the right to work. It also urged the legislature to review the rule from time to time.
raw.held: The rule that an appraiser's office is limited to one location, with no branch offices, does not violate the proportionality principle in Article 23 of the Constitution and is consistent with the protection of the right to work in Article 15.

points.text: The ban limits how appraisers practice, so it touches the freedom to carry out an occupation. Because appraisers' work closely affects the public interest and people's property, the state may regulate it. A restriction is acceptable if it serves the public interest and has a reasonable link to that goal.

The goal is legitimate. Appraisal quality affects transaction safety and the economy. A single office makes oversight unified, keeps responsibility matched to the named appraiser, and helps prevent lending out one's license, which protects clients' property and the financial market.

The ban has a reasonable link to that goal. It lets the authorities check more effectively whether appraisers follow the law. It also reduces the incentive to hand appraisal work to others in breach of the rules.
Appraisers may practice nationwide from one office, so no exception for major public interest or emergencies is needed. This differs from the situation in Interpretation No. 711.
The court therefore concluded that the means have a reasonable link to the goal and do not violate Article 23 or Article 15.

The court noted that the rule affects administrative efficiency, but since the legislative intent is one office with nationwide practice, the legislature should review the rule in time. It should consider the profession's development, public trust, and how other professions treat branch offices.
